title: Why did lace cost as much as silk?
teaches: Needle lace and bobbin lace and how each is made; the cross and twist of bobbin lace; why lace took so many hours; Venice, Flanders and Colbert's royal workshops; lace schools; Heathcoat's bobbinet machine and the Nottingham lace trade

blocks.text: Portraits from the late 16th and 17th centuries show rich men and women in white ruffs and falling collars edged or made entirely of lace. Those collars were among the most expensive things the sitters owned, and in wills and inventories of the time a good lace collar could be valued as highly as jewellery. In this lesson we look at what lace is, the two ways it was made by hand, why it took so long, and how machines made it cheap in the 19th century.

**Lace** is an openwork cloth in which the holes are as much part of the design as the thread. It grew in the 16th century out of two kinds of decorated linen. In cutwork, holes were cut in a linen cloth and filled with embroidery; in drawn-thread work, threads were pulled out of the weave and the remaining threads bound into patterns. Lace makers then learned to do without the cloth altogether and build the whole pattern from thread.

**Needle lace** is made with a single needle and thread. The design is drawn on parchment, and its outline is tacked down, held with temporary stitches, with a heavier thread. The lace maker then fills the shapes with rows of tiny looped stitches, each one worked into the loops of the row before, and finally cuts the tacking to free the lace from the parchment. Venetian lace makers called it *punto in aria*, stitches in the air. Venice was the leading centre of needle lace in the 16th and 17th centuries.

**Bobbin lace** is made with many threads at once, each wound on a small wooden or bone bobbin that keeps it tidy and gives it weight. The threads hang in pairs from pins stuck into a firm cushion, called a pillow, over a paper pattern pricked with holes for the pins. The lace maker works by moving bobbins over one another and pins each finished stitch in place. Flanders, especially around Brussels, Mechelen and Bruges, was the great centre of bobbin lace.

However complex a bobbin lace looks, every stitch in it is built by repeating just two kinds of move on four bobbins, numbered one to four from the left. In a **cross**, bobbin two, the left middle one, passes over bobbin three, the right middle one. In a **twist**, the right bobbin of each pair passes over the left.

blocks.task: Find the moves that carry the tan pair through the blue pair

blocks.text: The three moves cross, twist, cross make a **cloth stitch**, in which one pair passes through another over and under, just as a weft passes through a warp. A lace maker repeats it with one travelling pair across a row of hanging pairs to make a solid, woven-looking area. Other combinations make open net grounds, plaits and twisted bars. A fine piece of Flemish lace used hundreds of bobbins at once.

Lace was expensive because of the hours. Every hole in a needle lace is outlined by dozens of tiny stitches, and every stitch in a bobbin lace is several moves of the bobbins. A skilled worker making fine lace might finish only a few square centimetres in a day, so a large collar could take many months. The thread added to the cost. The finest Flemish lace used linen thread spun so thin that, by tradition, spinners worked in damp cellars to keep it from breaking, and it was among the most expensive threads on the market.

Governments saw lace as a drain of money abroad, and France spent heavily on Venetian lace. In 1665 Jean-Baptiste Colbert, chief minister to Louis XIV of France, set up royal lace workshops in Alençon and other towns and brought in Venetian lace makers to train French women. Their lace, called *point de France*, soon replaced imports from Venice at the French court. England banned imports of Flemish lace for long periods, and smuggling was common.

Most lace was made by poor women and girls working at home or in small workshops, paid by the piece through dealers who supplied the thread and patterns. In the English lace districts of Devon and the East Midlands, children as young as five were sent to lace schools, where they worked at the pillow for many hours a day and learned little reading or writing.

Machines first made the net that formed the background of much lace. In 1809 **John Heathcoat** patented a bobbinet machine that twisted threads around one another to make a fine net like the ground of bobbin lace. Luddites, the machine breakers of branch lesson K4, smashed his machines in Loughborough in 1816, and he moved his factory to Tiverton in Devon, where it still works today. A few years later John Levers, whose machine became known as the Leavers, adapted a machine that could make the patterns as well as the net. Nottingham became the centre of machine lace, and by the middle of the 19th century machine lace imitated most handmade styles at a small fraction of the price.

Machine lace put lace on the curtains and petticoats of ordinary households, and the handmade trade shrank to a luxury and a craft. The story repeats what lesson 14 showed for hand spinning and lesson 18 for patterned weaving. Once a machine could make the same structure, the value of the hours spent by hand fell.

choices: One needle builds looped stitches over a tacked outline
Many bobbins are crossed and twisted on a pillow
Holes are punched into a finished linen cloth
A frame of hooks knits threads into loops
items.why: The outline is tacked to parchment, filled with stitches worked into earlier loops, then cut free.

items.ask: What does a cloth stitch in bobbin lace do?
choices: Passes one pair through another, like weaving
Ties all four threads into a single knot
Twists every thread around its neighbour once
Joins two finished pieces of lace together
items.why: Cross, twist, cross carries the travelling pair over and under the hanging pair.

items.ask: Why did Colbert set up royal lace workshops in France?
choices: To stop French money going to Venice for lace
To supply the French army with uniforms
To train lace makers for export to England
items.why: Lace was a costly import, and French-made point de France replaced Venetian lace at court.

items.ask: What did Heathcoat's machine make first?
choices: The fine net that formed lace's background
Linen thread for hand lace makers
Bobbins and pillows for lace schools
items.why: His bobbinet machine twisted threads into net. Machines that made the patterns came a few years later.

summary: **Lace is cloth made of holes.** It grew from cutwork and drawn-thread embroidery in the 16th century.
**Lace is made with a needle or bobbins.** Needle lace loops stitches into a tacked outline, as in Venice, while bobbin lace crosses and twists thread pairs on a pillow, as in Flanders.
**The hours made lace dear.** A lacemaker made a few square centimetres a day in costly fine linen thread, and women and children did the work at piece rates.
**Machines made lace cheap.** Heathcoat's bobbinet machine made net from 1809, and Nottingham's machines later made patterned lace.
